claim: A high portion of the earliest known insect fauna is composed of the so-called 'lobeattid insects'.
source: A high portion of the earliest known insect fauna is composed of the so-called 'lobeattid insects', whose systematic affinities and role as foliage feeders remain debated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about the composition of early insect fauna.

claim: The systematic affinities of lobeattid insects remain debated.
source: A high portion of the earliest known insect fauna is composed of the so-called 'lobeattid insects', whose systematic affinities and role as foliage feeders remain debated.
evidence: This is stated as an ongoing debate in the field.

claim: The role of lobeattid insects as foliage feeders remains debated.
source: A high portion of the earliest known insect fauna is composed of the so-called 'lobeattid insects', whose systematic affinities and role as foliage feeders remain debated.
evidence: This is stated as an ongoing debate in the field.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. possessed a sword-shaped ovipositor with valves interlocked by two ball-and-socket mechanisms.
source: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. possessed a sword-shaped ovipositor with valves interlocked by two ball-and-socket mechanisms, lacked jumping hind-legs, and certain wing venation features.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fossil specimens described in the study.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. lacked jumping hind-legs.
source: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. possessed a sword-shaped ovipositor with valves interlocked by two ball-and-socket mechanisms, lacked jumping hind-legs, and certain wing venation features.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fossil specimens described in the study.

claim: The combination of characters in Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. unambiguously supports lobeattids as stem relatives of all living Orthoptera.
source: This combination of characters unambiguously supports lobeattids as stem relatives of all living Orthoptera (crickets, grasshoppers, katydids).
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological characters observed in the fossil specimens and comparative analysis.

claim: Lobeattids experienced an early diversification.
source: Given the herein presented and other remains, it follows that this group experienced an early diversification and, additionally, occurred in high individual numbers.
evidence: This is inferred from the fossil evidence presented in the study and other remains.

claim: Lobeattids occurred in high individual numbers.
source: Given the herein presented and other remains, it follows that this group experienced an early diversification and, additionally, occurred in high individual numbers.
evidence: This is inferred from the fossil evidence presented in the study and other remains.

claim: The ovipositor shape of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. indicates that ground was the preferred substrate for eggs.
source: The ovipositor shape indicates that ground was the preferred substrate for eggs.
evidence: This is inferred from comparative analysis of ovipositor morphology with extant species.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. was likely omnivorous.
source: The new species was likely omnivorous which explains the paucity of external damage on contemporaneous plant foliage.
evidence: This is inferred from biomechanical analysis of mandibular morphology compared to extant species.

claim: The omnivorous nature of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. explains the paucity of external damage on contemporaneous plant foliage.
source: The new species was likely omnivorous which explains the paucity of external damage on contemporaneous plant foliage.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the dietary habits to the fossil record of plant damage.

claim: The earliest known insect fauna in the Pennsylvanian occurred ca. 307 million years ago.
source: The earliest known insect fauna in the Pennsylvanian, ca. 307 million years ago, was composed by species displaying mixtures of inherited (plesiomorphic) and derived (apomorphic) conditions, such as the griffenflies (stem relatives of dragon- and damselflies), but also by highly specialized groups, such as the gracile and sap-feeding megasecopterans, belonging to the extinct taxon Rostropalaeoptera.
evidence: This is a statement about the geological age of the fauna, based on established knowledge.

claim: The earliest known insect fauna in the Pennsylvanian was composed by species displaying mixtures of inherited (plesiomorphic) and derived (apomorphic) conditions.
source: The earliest known insect fauna in the Pennsylvanian, ca. 307 million years ago, was composed by species displaying mixtures of inherited (plesiomorphic) and derived (apomorphic) conditions, such as the griffenflies (stem relatives of dragon- and damselflies), but also by highly specialized groups, such as the gracile and sap-feeding megasecopterans, belonging to the extinct taxon Rostropalaeoptera.
evidence: This is a general statement about the composition of the fauna, based on established knowledge.

claim: Griffenflies are stem relatives of dragon- and damselflies.
source: The earliest known insect fauna in the Pennsylvanian, ca. 307 million years ago, was composed by species displaying mixtures of inherited (plesiomorphic) and derived (apomorphic) conditions, such as the griffenflies (stem relatives of dragon- and damselflies), but also by highly specialized groups, such as the gracile and sap-feeding megasecopterans, belonging to the extinct taxon Rostropalaeoptera.
evidence: This is a statement about phylogenetic relationships, based on established knowledge.

claim: Megasecopterans belong to the extinct taxon Rostropalaeoptera.
source: The earliest known insect fauna in the Pennsylvanian, ca. 307 million years ago, was composed by species displaying mixtures of inherited (plesiomorphic) and derived (apomorphic) conditions, such as the griffenflies (stem relatives of dragon- and damselflies), but also by highly specialized groups, such as the gracile and sap-feeding megasecopterans, belonging to the extinct taxon Rostropalaeoptera.
evidence: This is a statement about taxonomic classification, based on established knowledge.

claim: Lobeattid insects have been recovered from all major Pennsylvanian outcrops.
source: They have been recovered from all major Pennsylvanian outcrops, where some species can abound (Béthoux, 2005c; Béthoux, 2008; Béthoux and Nel, 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some lobeattid species can abound at Pennsylvanian outcrops.
source: They have been recovered from all major Pennsylvanian outcrops, where some species can abound (Béthoux, 2005c; Béthoux, 2008; Béthoux and Nel, 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At the Xiaheyan locality, lobeattid insects collectively account for more than half of all insect occurrences.
source: Indeed, at the Xiaheyan locality, China, for which quantitative data are available, they collectively account for more than half of all insect occurrences (Trümper et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study providing quantitative data.

claim: Cnemidolestodea is composed of derived relatives of lobeattid insects.
source: Additionally, another extinct group, the Cnemidolestodea, composed of derived relatives of lobeattid insects, was likewise ubiquitously distributed during the Pennsylvanian until the onset of the Permian (Béthoux, 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cnemidolestodea was ubiquitously distributed during the Pennsylvanian until the onset of the Permian.
source: Additionally, another extinct group, the Cnemidolestodea, composed of derived relatives of lobeattid insects, was likewise ubiquitously distributed during the Pennsylvanian until the onset of the Permian (Béthoux, 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lobeattid insects have been regarded as stem relatives of Orthoptera.
source: They have been regarded as stem relatives of either Orthoptera (crickets, grasshoppers, katydids; Béthoux and Nel, 2002; Béthoux and Nel, 2005a) or of several other lineages within the diverse Polyneoptera (Aristov, 2014; Rasnitsyn, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lobeattid insects have been regarded as stem relatives of several other lineages within the diverse Polyneoptera.
source: They have been regarded as stem relatives of either Orthoptera (crickets, grasshoppers, katydids; Béthoux and Nel, 2002; Béthoux and Nel, 2005a) or of several other lineages within the diverse Polyneoptera (Aristov, 2014; Rasnitsyn, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A core point of the debate about lobeattid phylogenetic affinities is the presumed wing venation ground pattern of insects.
source: A core point of the debate is the presumed wing venation ground pattern of insects, which, however, will remain elusive until Mississipian or even earlier fossil wings are discovered.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the debate and the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: The wing venation ground pattern of insects will remain elusive until Mississipian or even earlier fossil wings are discovered.
source: A core point of the debate is the presumed wing venation ground pattern of insects, which, however, will remain elusive until Mississipian or even earlier fossil wings are discovered.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future discoveries needed to resolve the debate.

claim: Lobeattid insects have been traditionally regarded as foliage feeders.
source: Traditionally, they have been regarded as foliage feeders (Labandeira, 1998) but, given their abundance, this is in contrast to the paucity of documented external foliage damage during that time.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The abundance of lobeattid insects is in contrast to the paucity of documented external foliage damage during the Pennsylvanian.
source: Traditionally, they have been regarded as foliage feeders (Labandeira, 1998) but, given their abundance, this is in contrast to the paucity of documented external foliage damage during that time.
evidence: This is an observation that creates a paradox requiring explanation.

claim: The Xiaheyan locality contains a large amount of insect material.
source: The Xiaheyan locality is unique in several respects (Trümper et al., 2020), including the amount of insect material it contains.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Over the past decade, a collection of several thousand insect specimens was unearthed from the Xiaheyan locality.
source: Over the past decade, a collection of several thousand specimens was unearthed, allowing for highly detailed analyses of, for example, ovipositor and mouthparts morphology of extinct insect lineages (Pecharová et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a statement about the collection effort and its results.

claim: The large collection from Xiaheyan allows for highly detailed analyses of ovipositor and mouthparts morphology of extinct insect lineages.
source: Over the past decade, a collection of several thousand specimens was unearthed, allowing for highly detailed analyses of, for example, ovipositor and mouthparts morphology of extinct insect lineages (Pecharová et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and the current study's methodology.

claim: The etymology of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. is based on 'frequens' ('frequent' in Latin), referring to the abundance of the species at the Xiaheyan locality.
source: Based on 'frequens' ('frequent' in Latin), referring to the abundance of the species at the Xiaheyan locality.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the naming of the species.

claim: The holotype of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. is specimen CNU-NX1-326.
source: Holotype. Specimen CNU-NX1-326 (female individual; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the holotype designation.

claim: The holotype of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. is a female individual.
source: Holotype. Specimen CNU-NX1-326 (female individual; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sex of the holotype.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. is from the Xiaheyan Village, Zhongwei City, Yanghugou Formation (Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, China).
source: Xiaheyan Village, Zhongwei City, Yanghugou Formation (Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, China); latest Bashkirian (latest Duckmantian) to middle Moscovian (Bolsovian), early Pennsylvanian (Trümper et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the locality and horizon.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. is from the latest Bashkirian (latest Duckmantian) to middle Moscovian (Bolsovian), early Pennsylvanian.
source: Xiaheyan Village, Zhongwei City, Yanghugou Formation (Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, China); latest Bashkirian (latest Duckmantian) to middle Moscovian (Bolsovian), early Pennsylvanian (Trümper et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. is largely similar to Ctenoptilus elongatus (Brongniart, 1893), in particular in its wing venation.
source: The species is largely similar to Ctenoptilus elongatus (Brongniart, 1893), in particular in its wing venation (Appendix 1, Section 2.1.2).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on morphological analysis.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. differs from Ctenoptilus elongatus in its smaller size (deduced from forewing length).
source: However, it differs from it in its smaller size (deduced from forewing length) and its prothorax longer than wide (as opposed to quadrangular).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on morphological analysis.

claim: Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. differs from Ctenoptilus elongatus in its prothorax longer than wide (as opposed to quadrangular).
source: However, it differs from it in its smaller size (deduced from forewing length) and its prothorax longer than wide (as opposed to quadrangular).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on morphological analysis.

claim: The studied fossils of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. possess three pairs of valves in their ovipositor, each strongly sclerotized.
source: The studied fossils possess three pairs of valves in their ovipositor, each strongly sclerotized (Figure 2, and Appendix 1—figure 7B, C, 8B and C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fossil specimens, supported by figures.

claim: The valve margins are still visible in the anterior area ('base') of the ovipositor of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov.
source: Especially the valve margins are still visible in the anterior area ('base'), including the dorsal margin of the gonostylus IX (gs9), the ventral margin of the gonapophysis IX (gp9), and the dorsal and ventral margins of gonapophysis VIII (gp8).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: All observed ovipositors of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. display a thin longitudinal line from the second third of their length onwards, which is the primary olistheter (olis1).
source: All observed ovipositors, but in particular the one of specimen CNU-NX1-742 (Figure 2D–F, and Appendix 1—figure 8B and C), display, from the second third of their length onwards, a thin longitudinal line much sharper and more developed than other visible linear structures in the area. This is the primary olistheter (olis1), a tongue-like structure which commonly interlocks gp9 and gp8 in extant insects having more or less well-developed external ovipositors (Figure 3; Klass, 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fossil structure based on comparison with extant insects, supported by a citation.

claim: The primary olistheter (olis1) is a tongue-like structure which commonly interlocks gp9 and gp8 in extant insects having more or less well-developed external ovipositors.
source: This is the primary olistheter (olis1), a tongue-like structure which commonly interlocks gp9 and gp8 in extant insects having more or less well-developed external ovipositors (Figure 3; Klass, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the distal half of the ovipositor of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov., the linear structure occurring between the dorsal edge of gs9 and olis1 is interpreted as the dorsal margin of gp9.
source: In the distal half of the ovipositor, the linear structure occurring between the dorsal edge of gs9 and olis1 is interpreted as the dorsal margin of gp9.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fossil structure based on morphological analysis.

claim: The extent of olis1 in Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. indicates that gp9 reaches the ovipositor apex.
source: The extent of olis1 indicates that gp9 reaches the ovipositor apex, which is corroborated by the length of its inferred dorsal margin, well visible in specimen CNU-NX1-749 (Figure 2A, and Appendix 1—figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structure, corroborated by specific specimen observations.

claim: Specimen CNU-NX1-749 shows that gp8 bears ventrally oriented teeth, more prominent and densely distributed near the apex, as in many extant orthopterans.
source: This specimen also shows that gp8 bears ventrally oriented teeth, more prominent and densely distributed near the apex, as in many extant orthopterans.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fossil specimen, compared to extant species.

claim: The location of the dorsal margin of gp9 could not be observed with confidence near the base in Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov., which might be due to a lower degree of sclerotization.
source: The location of the dorsal margin of gp9 could not be observed with confidence near the base, which might be due to a lower degree of sclerotization.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of observation and a speculative explanation.

claim: At the base of the ovipositor of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov., dorsal to the anterior margin of gp8, only gs9 and gp9 occur.
source: This morphology implies that, at the base, dorsal to the anterior margin of gp8, only gs9 and gp9 occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed morphology.

claim: The sharp and heavily sclerotized longitudinal line, located slightly dorsally with respect to the ventral margin of gs9 in Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov., is a second olistheter (olis2) interlocking gs9 and gp9.
source: Therefore, the sharp and heavily sclerotized longitudinal line, located slightly dorsally with respect to the ventral margin of gs9, can only be an olistheter interlocking these two valves. This second olistheter (olis2) reaches olis1 but its development beyond this point could not be inferred with the available material.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed morphology and the constraints of the structure.

claim: The second olistheter (olis2) in Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. reaches olis1 but its development beyond this point could not be inferred with the available material.
source: This second olistheter (olis2) reaches olis1 but its development beyond this point could not be inferred with the available material.
evidence: This is a statement about the extent of observation and its limitations.

claim: The occurrence of a mechanism locking gs9 onto gp9 in Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. is supported by the fact that these valves remained connected to each other in specimen CNU-NX1-742 even though it endured heavy decay.
source: The occurrence of a mechanism locking gs9 onto gp9 is further supported by the fact that these valves remained connected to each other in the specimen CNU-NX1-742 even though it endured heavy decay (head and ovipositor detached from thorax and abdomen, respectively; Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is an inference based on the preservation state of a specific specimen.

claim: The head and mouthpart morphology of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. could be investigated in more detail in six specimens.
source: The head and mouthpart morphology could be investigated in more detail in six specimens (see Appendix 1) while we could study the mechanical advantage (MA; see Section 1.5 of Appendix 1) of their mandibles in four of the six (viz. CNU-NX1-326, −747,–754, –764).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology and sample size.

claim: The mechanical advantage (MA) of the mandibles of Ctenoptilus frequens sp. nov. was studied in four specimens (viz. CNU-NX1-326, −747,–754, –764).
source: The head and mouthpart morphology could be investigated in more detail in six specimens (see Appendix 1) while we could study the mechanical advantage (MA; see Section 1.5 of Appendix 1) of their mandibles in four of the six (viz. CNU-NX1-326, −747,–754, –764).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology and sample size.

claim: The MA is defined as the inlever to outlever ratio and thus indicates the percentage of force transmitted to the food item.
source: The MA is defined as the inlever to outlever ratio and thus indicates the percentage of force transmitted to the food item (i.e. the effectivity of the lever system).
evidence: This is a definition of a biomechanical concept.

claim: The MA allows for a size-independent comparison of the relative efficiencies of force transmission to the food item.
source: Therefore, the MA allows for a size-independent comparison of the relative efficiencies of force transmission to the food item.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the MA metric.

claim: Low MA values usually indicate quick biting with low force transmission typical for predators.
source: Low MA values usually indicate quick biting with low force transmission typical for predators, while high MA values indicate comparatively slow biting with higher force transmission typical for non-predatory species.
evidence: This is a general statement about the interpretation of MA values, based on established knowledge.

claim: High MA values usually indicate comparatively slow biting with higher force transmission typical for non-predatory species.
source: Low MA values usually indicate quick biting with low force transmission typical for predators, while high MA values indicate comparatively slow biting with higher force transmission typical for non-predatory species.
evidence: This is a general statement about the interpretation of MA values, based on established knowledge.

claim: Calculation of the MA along the entire gnathal edge revealed characteristic MA curve progressions for the studied taxa.
source: Calculation of the MA along the entire gnathal edge revealed characteristic MA curve progressions for the studied taxa (Appendix 1, Section 2.3, and Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This is a statement about the results of the analysis.

claim: Compared to the studied fossils, extant Dermaptera, Embioptera, and Phasmatodea showed comparatively high MAs with an almost linear curve progression towards more distal parts of the mandibular incisivi.
source: Compared to the studied fossils, extant Dermaptera, Embioptera, and Phasmatodea showed comparatively high MAs with an almost linear curve progression towards more distal parts of the mandibular incisivi whereas Plecoptera, Zoraptera, and Grylloblattodea were located at the lower end of the MA range with a gently exponential decrease towards the distal incisivi.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the analysis of extant species.

claim: Plecoptera, Zoraptera, and Grylloblattodea were located at the lower end of the MA range with a gently exponential decrease towards the distal incisivi.
source: Compared to the studied fossils, extant Dermaptera, Embioptera, and Phasmatodea showed comparatively high MAs with an almost linear curve progression towards more distal parts of the mandibular incisivi whereas Plecoptera, Zoraptera, and Grylloblattodea were located at the lower end of the MA range with a gently exponential decrease towards the distal incisivi.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on the analysis of extant species.

claim: The analysed extant Orthoptera occupy a comparatively wide functional space, with lineages at the higher and lower ends of the MA range.
source: The analysed extant Orthoptera occupy a comparatively wide functional space, with lineages at the higher and lower ends of the MA range.
evidence: This is a statement about the diversity of MA values in extant Orthoptera.

claim: The composite fossil mandible representation (CFMR) of Ct. frequens is located in the centre of the observed range of MAs for Orthoptera.
source: The composite fossil mandible representation (CFMR) of Ct. frequens (see Materials and methods) is located in the centre of the observed range of MAs for Orthoptera (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statement about the position of the fossil in the comparative analysis, supported by a figure.

claim: A polynomial function of the fifth order resulted in the best relative fit on the MA curves according to the Akaike information criterion (AIC) value (–661.3).
source: A polynomial function of the fifth order resulted in the best relative fit on the MA curves according to the Akaike information criterion (AIC) value (–661.3, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis performed.

claim: Phylogenetic signal was detected in the MA data (K = 1.03316; p = 0.0001).
source: The five common coefficients were subjected to a principal component analysis (PCA, Figure 4E), and, because phylogenetic signal was detected (K = 1.03316; p = 0.0001), also analysed using a phylogenetic principal component analysis (pPCA) (Appendix 1, Section 2.3, and Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis performed.

claim: The first four principal components (PCs) accounted for 96.8% (PCA)/96% (pPCA) of the variation in MA.
source: The first four principal components (PCs) accounted for 96.8% (PCA)/96% (pPCA) of the variation in MA (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the results of the PCA analysis.

claim: In both PCAs, PC1 mainly codes for the vertical position of the MA curve, that is, the effectivity of the force transmission along the whole toothrow.
source: In both PCAs, PC1 mainly codes for the vertical position of the MA curve, that is, the effectivity of the force transmission along the whole toothrow, while PC2 mainly codes for the curvature, that is, whether there is an almost linear or a gently exponential decrease in the effectivity of force transmission.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results.

claim: PC2 mainly codes for the curvature, that is, whether there is an almost linear or a gently exponential decrease in the effectivity of force transmission.
source: In both PCAs, PC1 mainly codes for the vertical position of the MA curve, that is, the effectivity of the force transmission along the whole toothrow, while PC2 mainly codes for the curvature, that is, whether there is an almost linear or a gently exponential decrease in the effectivity of force transmission.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results.

claim: Due to the narrow distribution of species along PC3, it was not possible to associate a clear biomechanical pattern to this PC.
source: Due to the narrow distribution of species along PC3, it was not possible to associate a clear biomechanical pattern to this PC.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the PCA interpretation.

claim: The CFMR of Ct. frequens is located at the centre of the first three PCs.
source: The CFMR of Ct. frequens is located at the centre of the first three PCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a statement about the position of the fossil in the PCA, supported by a figure.

claim: Omnivorous Orthoptera and all herbivore taxa, with the exception of Apotrechus, are located along the width of PC1.
source: Omnivorous Orthoptera and all herbivore taxa, with the exception of Apotrechus, are located along the width of PC1, while there is a tendency for the carnivorous taxa within the sampling to be spread along PC2.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of dietary groups in the PCA.

claim: There is a tendency for the carnivorous taxa within the sampling to be spread along PC2.
source: Omnivorous Orthoptera and all herbivore taxa, with the exception of Apotrechus, are located along the width of PC1, while there is a tendency for the carnivorous taxa within the sampling to be spread along PC2.
evidence: This is a statement about the distribution of dietary groups in the PCA.

claim: The analysis of material of Ct. frequens provides unequivocal evidence that olis2 occurs in this species.
source: Our analysis of material of Ct. frequens provides unequivocal evidence that olis2 occurs in this species.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the morphological analysis.

claim: The new species Ct. frequens was an orthopteran.
source: Therefore, the new species was an orthopteran.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the presence of olis2.

claim: The ovipositor configuration in Ct. elongatus conforms to that observed in extant cave crickets (Raphidophoridae) in which olis2 occurs in addition to olis1 and interlocks gs9 and gp9.
source: The ovipositor configuration in Ct. elongatus furthermore conforms that observed in extant cave crickets (Raphidophoridae) in which olis2 occurs in addition to olis1 and interlocks gs9 and gp9 (Figure 3A–C; Appendix 1, Section 2.2).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on morphological analysis.

claim: Olis2 is present in ensiferan ('sword-bearing') Orthoptera possessing a developed ovipositor.
source: Indeed, this structure is present in ensiferan ('sword-bearing') Orthoptera possessing a developed ovipositor and is absent in caeliferan ('chisel-bearing') Orthoptera (Cappe de Baillon, 1920; Cappe de Baillon, 1922; Kluge, 2016; and see below).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Olis2 is absent in caeliferan ('chisel-bearing') Orthoptera.
source: Indeed, this structure is present in ensiferan ('sword-bearing') Orthoptera possessing a developed ovipositor and is absent in caeliferan ('chisel-bearing') Orthoptera (Cappe de Baillon, 1920; Cappe de Baillon, 1922; Kluge, 2016; and see below).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The new species Ct. frequens is either more closely related to Ensifera than to Caelifera (owing to the possession of olis2), or it is a stem-orthopteran and olis2 was secondarily lost in Caelifera.
source: It follows that the new species is either more closely related to Ensifera than to Caelifera (owing to the possession of olis2), or it is a stem-orthopteran and olis2 was secondarily lost in Caelifera.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic implications of the presence of olis2.

claim: Ct. frequens lacked jump-related specializations in the hind-leg.
source: Further evidence for the phylogenetic placement of Ct. frequens is based on the lack of jump-related specializations in the hind-leg.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: Jump-related specializations in the hind-leg define the taxon Saltatoria within Orthoptera.
source: Such specializations define the taxon Saltatoria within Orthoptera, and therefore Ct. frequens can be confidently excluded from crown-Orthoptera.
evidence: This is a statement about the defining characteristics of Saltatoria, based on established knowledge.

claim: Ct. frequens can be confidently excluded from crown-Orthoptera.
source: Such specializations define the taxon Saltatoria within Orthoptera, and therefore Ct. frequens can be confidently excluded from crown-Orthoptera.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of jump-related specializations.

claim: Ct. frequens lacked a forked CuPa vein before its fusion with the CuA vein.
source: This conclusion is furthermore corroborated by wing vein characteristics: Ct. frequens lacked a forked CuPa vein before its fusion with the CuA vein.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the fossil specimens.

claim: A forked CuPa vein is typical for Panorthoptera, which includes crown-Orthoptera and their nearest stem relatives.
source: Such a forked CuPa vein is typical for Panorthoptera, which includes crown-Orthoptera and their nearest stem relatives (Béthoux and Nel, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ct. frequens, and its various Pennsylvanian relatives collectively referred to as 'lobeattid insects' are stem relatives of Orthoptera.
source: Given this evidence, based on the configuration of several body parts, Ct. frequens, and its various Pennsylvanian relatives collectively referred to as 'lobeattid insects' are stem relatives of Orthoptera (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of morphological evidence.

claim: The absence of olis2 in Caelifera is the consequence of a secondary loss.
source: The absence of olis2 in Caelifera therefore is the consequence of a secondary loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic placement of Ct. frequens.

claim: Based only on extant species, the evolution of the external ovipositor in crown-Orthoptera was ambiguous due to the organizational diversity of its substructures.

source: Orthoptera possess a variety of additional olistheters, including one interlocking gs9 onto gp9 (royal blue in Figures 2 and 3; olis2), commonly present in ensiferans possessing a well-developed ovipositor, as exemplified by Rhaphidophoridae (cave crickets; Figure 2E, igure 3A and B, and see sections labelled 'a–c' on Figure 3C), and Gryllacrididae (raspy and king crickets) and Anostostomatidae (king crickets) (Figure 2 G3C).

claim: In Rhaphidophoridae, gs9 extends more ventrally, concealing gp8 for some distance.

claim: Compared to Gryllacrididae the only notable difference in Ct. frequens is the ventral extension of gs9 in the former.

source: Gs9 and gp8 are connected by an olistheter and we suggest that it might represent a variant of olis2, assuming a hypothetical case (shaded scheme in Figure 3C) in which olis2 interlocks gs9, gp9, and gp8 altogether.

claim: Caelifera use valves for digging a tunnel to accommodate their entire abdomen and, additionally, dig egg pods.
source: Unlike other orthopterans displaying a well-developed external ovipositor, Caelifera use valves for digging a tunnel to accommodate their entire abdomen and, additionally, dig egg pods (Fedorov, 1927; Stauffer and Whitman, 1997; Uvarov, 1966).

claim: The shoving operation to move forward in Caelifera is accomplished by powerful, rhythmic, dorso-ventral openings and closings of two sets of valves (gs9 and gp8+ gp9).
source: The shoving operation to move forward is accomplished by powerful, rhythmic, dorso-ventral openings and closings of two sets of valves (Thompson, 1986), gs9 and gp8+ gp9, the two latter ones being interlocked via olis1.

claim: In Caelifera, gp8 and gp9 are interlocked via olis1.

claim: Even though gp9 is often reduced in Caelifera, it plays an important role in the closing of the ovipositor via muscles attached to it.
source: Even though gp9 is often reduced, it plays an important role in the closing of the ovipositor via muscles attached to it (Thompson, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The loss of olis2 in Caelifera is a likely consequence of their highly derived oviposition technique.

claim: Rock-crawlers can be understood as possessing an elongate ovipositor, which would render the term 'Ensifera' ambiguous.

claim: It is proposed to coin a new taxon name, Neoclavifera, to encompass species bearing an olis2, that is, all extant orthopterans and their stem relatives as currently known.

claim: The phylogeny adopted for comparative analyses is based on the most comprehensive account to date.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MA was extracted from 43 extant polyneopteran species including 31 orthopterans and one CFMR of the newly described fossil species.

claim: The CFMR was derived from a Procrustes superimposition of four fossil specimens which showed low levels of overall distortion and a mandible orientation suitable for extraction of individual MAs.
source: The CFMR was derived from a Procrustes superimposition (R package 'geomorph' v.3.0.5; Adams et al., 2013) of four fossil specimens which showed low levels of overall distortion and a mandible orientation suitable for extraction of individual MAs (Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology.

claim: A PCA and, due to the detection of significant phylogenetic signal, a pPCA were performed for comparison of species and inference of the dietary niche.
source: For comparison of species and inference of the dietary niche, a PCA and, due to the detection of significant phylogenetic signal, a pPCA (R package 'phytools' v.0.6–44; Revell, 2012) were performed (for results of the pPCA, see Appendix 1—figure 9, Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology.
